lead: In an emergency the skipper gives the orders, but the first seconds often belong to whoever is nearest. Learn the first actions by heart, and how to call for help if the skipper cannot.

qa.q: What should I do first if someone falls overboard?
qa.a: Shout "Man overboard!", throw the lifebuoy and danbuoy, point at the person without looking away, and press the plotter's **MOB** button to mark the position. The radio call comes after these four.

list: **Shout** "Man overboard!" so that everyone knows, and keep your eyes on the person.
**Throw** the lifebuoy and the danbuoy towards them at once: something to hold on to, and a marker you can see.
**Point**: one person is the spotter, who keeps an arm stretched out at the casualty and never looks away until they are alongside.
**Mark**: press the MOB button on the plotter. It saves the position where the person went in and shows the way back.

fig.note: The boat turns back; the spotter keeps pointing

blocks.p: A head among the waves is very easy to lose, which is why the alarm, the buoys and the marked position come before anything else. The radio call comes after them. If it is the skipper who is in the water, you do the same four things.

sections.title: The right answer for each fire

qa.q: Can I put water on a burning pan of oil on a boat?
qa.a: No: water makes burning oil erupt. Turn the gas off and cover the pan with the **fire blanket**. Fuel fires need powder, foam or CO2, wiring needs the power off first, and only fabric, wood or paper takes water.

blocks.p: What you put on a fire depends on what is burning. Water is right for some fires and makes others much worse.

head: What burns
Use
Never
rows: Oil or fat in a pan
Gas off, cover with the fire blanket
Power off, then powder or CO2

fig.title: You find a fire

Aim at the base of the flames

qa.q: There's water over the floorboards: how do I tell where it's coming from?
qa.a: Taste it: salt water means the sea is getting in, so check the **seacocks** and their hoses, the heads and the engine space. Fresh water means a leaking tank or pipe, which empties the tank but will not sink you.

blocks.p: Water over the floorboards: tell the skipper at once, then help to look for the source. Pumps only buy time; finding and stopping the leak saves the boat.

blocks.cap: Below the waterline: where the sea can get in.

blocks.p: **Taste the water.** Salt means the sea is coming in: look at the seacocks and their hoses, the heads and the engine space. Fresh means the boat's own water tank or its pipes are leaking, which empties the tank but will not sink you.

qa.q: How do I send a MAYDAY on the VHF if the skipper can't?
qa.a: Press and hold the red **DISTRESS** button until the set confirms, then on channel 16, high power, say MAYDAY three times, the yacht's name three times, your position, what is wrong, the help needed, people aboard, and OVER.

blocks.p: If the skipper cannot make the call, you must. First the red **DISTRESS** button under its flap: press and hold it until the set confirms. It sends an automatic alert with the boat's identity and, if a GPS is connected, her position.
Then your voice: **channel 16**, **high power** for the longest range. Press the button on the microphone to talk and let go to listen.
The **position** comes first, read off the plotter, so that help can set out even if the radio then fails. Speak slowly. No answer: say it again.

sections.title: What to do until help comes

qa.q: How do I treat a burn or scald on a boat?
qa.a: Cool the **burn** under running water for 20 minutes, then cover it loosely with cling film, and tell the skipper, who can get medical advice by radio.

blocks.p: You are not the doctor. Make the person safe, do the simple right thing and tell the skipper, who can get medical advice by radio.

head: Problem
Signs
What you do
rows: Hard shivering, blue lips after time in the water
Shelter, dry clothes, blankets, a warm sweet drink if alert. No alcohol
Cool running water for 20 minutes, then cover loosely with cling film
Confusion, the same question again and again
Keep them still, watch them, tell the skipper now
Headache, dizziness, heavy sweat, pale clammy skin
Shade, lie down, cool with water, sips of fluid
Sick for hours, keeps no water down, little urine
Small sips often; tell the skipper

blocks.p: Someone **unconscious but breathing** normally goes on their side in the recovery position: the airway stays open and vomit can drain out. Stay with them.

qa.q: When should we leave the yacht and get into the liferaft?
qa.a: Only on the skipper's order, when the yacht is really going down: stay with her as long as she floats, since she is bigger, drier and easier to see. You step up into the **liferaft**, not down.

blocks.p: The yacht is the best lifeboat you have: bigger, drier, easier to see, with water, food and a radio. A liferaft is small, wet and cold. So you leave only on the skipper's order, when the yacht is really going down.

head: Situation
What you do
rows: Damaged or taking water, but afloat
Stay aboard: pump, call for help, get the raft ready

blocks.rule: Stay with the yacht as long as she floats. You should step up into the liferaft, not down.
